differences.title: 1. Execution Model
differences.leftDesc: Temporal workers actively run and manage workflow state, resuming from the last known point upon failure, ensuring exactly-once execution semantics.
differences.rightDesc: Airflow executes tasks sequentially within a DAG, retrying failed tasks. State is managed by the scheduler, not within workers themselves.

differences.title: 2. Fault Tolerance
differences.leftDesc: Temporal workflows can automatically replay events from their history, allowing workers to process them deterministically even after restarts or failures.
differences.rightDesc: Airflow relies on explicit retry configurations for tasks and relies on the scheduler to reschedule failed tasks within the DAG.

differences.title: 3. State Management
differences.leftDesc: Temporal durably stores workflow state in its event history, enabling robust recovery and long-running processes without external databases for workflow state.
differences.rightDesc: Airflow stores task states and DAG run information in a relational database, which is crucial for its scheduling and monitoring.

differences.title: 4. Programming Model
differences.leftDesc: Temporal allows writing workflows directly in general-purpose programming languages (Go, Java, Python, etc.), making them code-first and easier to test.
differences.rightDesc: Airflow uses Python to define Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), often involving specific Airflow operators and a more declarative style.

differences.title: 5. Scalability
differences.leftDesc: Temporal scales by adding more stateless workers that connect to the cluster, processing tasks and workflows independently.
differences.rightDesc: Airflow scales by distributing tasks across different executors (Celery, Kubernetes) and scaling the scheduler components.

differences.title: 6. Long-Running Processes
differences.leftDesc: Temporal is designed for inherently long-running processes, handling complex state transitions and timers over extended periods reliably.
differences.rightDesc: Airflow excels at scheduled batch processing and ETL jobs, though it can be configured for longer runs with careful design.

differences.title: 7. Use Cases
differences.leftDesc: Ideal for microservices orchestration, complex business logic, human-in-the-loop processes, and mission-critical distributed system coordination.
differences.rightDesc: Primarily used for defining, scheduling, and monitoring data ETL pipelines, data warehousing tasks, and machine learning workflows.
